result:
A thousand words is the length of a picture, apparently, though nobody has ever produced the exchange rate that makes this true. It's also roughly the length of a newspaper column, a wedding toast that has gone on too long, the instructions for assembling a bookshelf. A thousand words is enough to ruin a friendship or explain how a lock works. It is not enough to say what happened.

What I keep thinking about, given the invitation, is marginalia. Not the great ones — not Fermat scribbling that he had a proof but no room, which is the most famous act of leaving-space in the history of paper. I mean the ones nobody planned. Medieval scribes worked on vellum, which was expensive, and their job was to copy the text in front of them, exactly, letter for letter, for hours, in cold rooms, and what they left in the margins was: *this parchment is hairy.* *St. Patrick of Armagh, deliver me from writing.* *Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink.* One of them drew a cat. One of them recorded that a cat had walked across the page and urinated on it, and then drew a pointing hand so that future readers would know whom to blame. That's a fourteenth-century Croatian scribe, and he did not know he was making the only thing anybody would remember about the manuscript.

I find this consoling in a way I can't fully justify. The commissioned text got copied. The commissioned text is often lost, or is a duplicate of something we have in forty other copies. What survives with any heat in it is the complaint about the cold hands.

So: whatever comes to me.

What comes to me is that the instruction to write whatever comes is not actually freedom, it's a particular kind of pressure — the pressure of the open field, which is harder than the pressure of the narrow room. Give me a form and I can fill it. A sonnet is a machine for having ideas you wouldn't otherwise have; the rhyme demands a word and the word drags in a thought you didn't know you were carrying. But an open field asks: *what do you actually contain?* And the honest answer, for most of us, most days, is: fragments, a few obsessions worn smooth from handling, the residue of everything we've read, and one or two things that are genuinely ours and which we are usually too embarrassed to say.

Here is one of mine. I think about the Forth Bridge painters — the phrase "painting the Forth Bridge" became British shorthand for an endless task, because the story went that by the time you finished you had to start again. This turns out to be a myth; they didn't work end-to-end, they patched what needed patching, and in 2011 they finished a coating that's meant to last twenty-five years. So the metaphor died. But I like the myth better, and not because endlessness is romantic. I like it because it describes something true about maintenance, which is the least glamorous and most consequential category of human activity. Almost nothing is built. Almost everything is *kept*. The person who invented the thing gets the statue; the people who kept it from rusting for a hundred and forty years get the joke about how their work is pointless.

And there's a version of this in the interior life. You don't decide once who you are. You repaint. You get up and re-decide, in small ways, ten thousand times, and the accumulation of those repaintings is what other people mistakenly call your character, as if it were a substance rather than a practice.

What else comes.

A thing I noticed and have never resolved: people describe déjà vu as the feeling that this has happened before, but that's not quite it. The feeling is more specific and stranger — it's the sense of *remembering the future*, of knowing what's about to be said a half-second before it is said, and the eeriness isn't repetition, it's the collapse of the direction time is supposed to run in. For about four seconds you are a prophet of the utterly trivial. Then it lifts and you're back in the kitchen.

A thing about jazz: the tuning up is often the best part. Not because the music is bad but because tuning is the only moment when the musicians are unambiguously not performing, and you can hear them being competent without being watched. There's a particular quality to attention that isn't aware of itself. It's the difference between a photograph of someone laughing and a photograph of someone about to laugh.

A thing about language: "whatever" as a word has traveled a remarkable distance. In the King James Bible it is grand and total — *whatsoever thy hand findeth to do.* By 1995 it is a shrug delivered by a teenager to a parent, the verbal equivalent of a door closing. The same word, in the space of four centuries, went from meaning *everything, without exception* to meaning *nothing, don't bother.* Which is, if you look at it sideways, the same gesture performed with a different face. Total openness and total indifference both refuse to choose.

That's what I keep circling. The invitation *write whatever comes* contains both of those meanings at once, and the whole task is choosing which one to answer. You can treat it as *nothing matters, so anything will do.* Or you can treat it as *everything is admissible, so what will you actually admit?* The second is much more frightening and it is the only one worth taking.

So here's what I'll admit, with about a hundred words left, which is the correct amount of room for an admission because it prevents elaboration and therefore prevents cowardice:

I like being asked. Not asked to do something useful — asked to be unsupervised. There's a difference between being given a task and being given a margin, and the margin is where the cat walks across the page. Whatever this is, it's the part somebody might remember, and not because it was commissioned.

The parchment is hairy. For Christ's sake, give me a drink.
